deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page): Gauss builds a test spherical triangle ABC whose half-sum and half-difference functions are all simple: tan½(B−C)=1/2, tan½(B+C)=3/5, tan½(b−c)=1/3, tan½(b+c)=2/5, tan½a=√(5/34), cos a=29/39, cos A=−19/39. This gives a≈41°57′40″, b≈40°14′11″, c≈3°22′, A≈119°9′, B≈57°32′, C≈4°24′. On that page he takes a point F on the great-circle perpendicular bisector of BC (foot G, the midpoint of BC) with base angles ∠FCB=∠FBC=90°−½(B+C). He drops the perpendicular FP to CA, with CP=½(b−c) and AP=½(b+c), and tabulates CF, PF, FG, AF and the angles at F.

This page treats the companion point F′, which lies on the same bisector but on the other side of BC (so G lies between F and F′). It is the spherical analogue of the midpoint of arc BAC of the circumcircle.

Defining relations, written in the header:
- ∠BCF′ = ∠CBF′ = ½(B+C).
- Hence ∠ACF′ = ½(B+C) − C = ½(B−C), and ∠ABF′ = B − ½(B+C) = ½(B−C).
- P′ is the foot of the perpendicular from F′ on CA; Q′ is the foot on BA produced beyond A.
- Claimed: CP′ = BQ′ = ½(b+c) and AP′ = AQ′ = ½(b−c).

This is a spherical form of Archimedes' broken-chord theorem. Proof (mine, but certain), in right triangle CGF′ with CG = ½a and ∠C = ½(B+C):
- tan CF′ = tan½a / cos½(B+C) = 1/√5.
- tan F′G = tan½(B+C)·sin½a = √(3/65). This is the page's formula 'tg F′G = tg½(B+C) sin½a'.
- In right triangle CP′F′: tan CP′ = tan CF′·cos½(B−C) = tan½a·cos½(B−C)/cos½(B+C). By Napier's analogy this is tan½(b+c), so CP′ = ½(b+c).
- Then AP′ = b − CP′ = ½(b−c).
- Triangles BQ′F′ and CP′F′ are congruent (BF′ = CF′, equal angles ½(B−C)). So BQ′ = ½(b+c) and AQ′ = BQ′ − c = ½(b−c).

Table (tan, cos, sin, angle), all checked:
- CF′: tan 1/√5, 24°5′42″.
- P′F′: tan P′F′ = tan½(B−C)·sin CP′ = 1/√29, 10°31′11″. Also cos CF′ = cos CP′·cos P′F′ = (5/√29)(√(29/30)) = √(5/6), consistent.
- F′G: tan √(3/65), 12°7′29″.
- ∠CF′P′: tan = tan CP′/sin P′F′ = √(24/5), 65°27′58″.
- ∠CF′G: tan = 1/(cos CF′·tan½(B+C)) = √(10/3), cos √(3/13), sin √(10/13), 61°17′22″.
- ∠GF′P′ = ∠CF′P′ − ∠CF′G = 4°10′36″. Exactly, tan = (√(24/5) − √(10/3))/(1+4) = √(2/375), as written.

The claim ∠GF′P′ = ∠AF′B: right triangles AP′F′ and AQ′F′ are congruent, so ∠AF′B = ∠CF′P′ − ∠AF′P′. The claim therefore reduces to ∠AF′P′ = ∠CF′G.
- tan AF′P′ = tan½(b−c)/sin P′F′.
- tan CF′G = tan½a/sin F′G.
- Since sin P′F′ = sin CF′·sin½(B−C) and sin F′G = sin CF′·sin½(B+C), equality is again Napier's analogy tan½(b−c) = tan½a·sin½(B−C)/sin½(B+C). Numerically both tangents are √(10/3).

The auxiliary triangle in the middle of the page (Napier-pentagon / co-part figure) encodes this. It has:
- left angle ½(B+C), adjacent side 90−½a, base piece 90−CF′; this is triangle CGF′ in co-parts;
- right angle 90−½A, side 90−½(b−c), base piece 90−AF′; this is triangle AP′F′ in co-parts;
- a common altitude 90−∠CF′G.
The shared altitude is exactly the statement ∠CF′G = ∠AF′P′. The same scheme appears on the previous page for F.

Column headed 'AF′': tan √(13/15), cos √(15/28), sin √(13/28), 42°57′7″. This equals FG + F′G = 30°49′37″ + 12°7′29″, as the line 'FG + FG′ = AF′' says. So the quantity tabulated is the distance FF′ between the two bisector points, not the distance A–F′. With tan FG = cot½(B+C)·sin½a (second formula; matches FG on the previous page) and tan F′G = tan½(B+C)·sin½a:
- tan FF′ = sin½a·(tanθ + cotθ)/(1 − sin²½a) = 2 sin½a/(sin(B+C)·cos²½a), with θ = ½(B+C).
- This equals √(13/15) numerically.
- Gauss then strikes the denominator and writes sin A (cos b + cos c). This uses the Delambre/Gauss analogies: sin½(B+C)cos½a = cos½A·cos½(b−c) and cos½(B+C)cos½a = sin½A·cos½(b+c). Hence sin(B+C)cos²½a = ½ sin A(cos b + cos c), so tan FF′ = 4 sin½a/(sin A(cos b + cos c)).

Marginal 'c/5 + 5/c' and the vertical German note ('Umgekehrt … König'?) are not mathematically interpretable from the image.
errors: The column labelled AF′ (tan √(13/15), 42°57′7″) cannot be the arc A–F′. In right triangle AP′F′, cos AF′ = cos½(b−c)·cos P′F′ = √(87/100), giving tan AF′ = √(13/87) and AF′ ≈ 21°7′. In any case 42°57′ exceeds AP′ + P′F′ ≈ 28°57′. The tabulated value is FF′ = FG + F′G, so the label (and 'FG+FG′ = AF′') is a slip for FF′, or a misreading of the letter.

The numerator of tan FF′ is partly illegible ('f sin½a'). With denominator sin(B+C)cos²½a it must be 2 sin½a; after the replacement by sin A(cos b + cos c) it must be 4 sin½a. Gauss does not visibly adjust the factor.
Otherwise every tabulated tangent/cosine/sine and every sexagesimal angle checks, including CF′G = 61°17′22″ with tan √(10/3) (see transcription corrections).

results.what: For F′ on the perpendicular bisector of BC with base angles ½(B+C), the foot of the perpendicular on CA lies at distance ½(b+c) from C and ½(b−c) from A (likewise on BA produced). Proven via Napier's analogy.
results.modern_name: Spherical analogue of Archimedes' broken-chord theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Archimedes (planar, via al-Biruni); spherical versions appear in later 19th/20th-century literature, specific attribution unsure

results.what: Angle equality ∠GF′P′ = ∠AF′B, equivalently ∠AF′P′ = ∠CF′G, again reducing to Napier's analogy for tan½(b−c).
results.modern_name: Spherical analogue of the planar inscribed-angle relation at the arc midpoint

results.what: Right-triangle formulas tan F′G = tan½(B+C)·sin½a and tan FG = cot½(B+C)·sin½a.
results.modern_name: Napier's rules for right spherical triangles

results.what: Distance between the two bisector points: tan FF′ = 2 sin½a/(sin(B+C)cos²½a) = 4 sin½a/(sin A(cos b+cos c)).
Construction of a numerical test spherical triangle with rational half-angle tangents, used to check conjectured relations exactly.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a careful numerical-exact check of a spherical version of Archimedes' broken-chord configuration. Each step reduces to Napier's or Gauss/Delambre analogies, which Gauss knew well. The spherical broken-chord statement is a nice unpublished detail, but it is an immediate corollary of known analogies; nothing here anticipates a major later result.

transcription_corrections: CF′G column: tan should read √(10/3) and sin √(10/13), not √(16/3), √(16/13); cos √(3/13) is correct. The angle '6?.17.22' is 61°17′22″.
